值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入了解 Anthropic 最新使用條款，釐清對 AI 的情緒發洩與惡意濫用之界線，避免帳號面臨停權風險。
  • 解析科技巨擘如馬斯克、微軟高層等對「AI 道德地位」與「是否該善待 AI」的哲學與實務爭論。
  • 透過華頓商學院等權威學術研究數據，揭露威脅、責罵與禮貌語氣對大語言模型表現的真實影響。
  • 掌握與 AI 溝通時容易犯下的三大邏輯陷阱，避免因情緒性指令與過長的多輪對話導致模型效能嚴重下滑。

摘要

Anthropic 推出新規：禁止虐待 AI 引發爭議

作者指出，過去科技圈常流傳「責罵 AI 會讓它更聰明且勤奮」的說法，但 Anthropic 近期更新了使用條款，正式禁止用戶對 Claude 進行持續且不必要的虐待或殘忍行為，違者可能面臨帳號停權。這項規定引發不少用戶恐慌，擔心稍微帶有情緒就會被封鎖。不過作者說明，官方已明確豁免了一般抱怨、質疑或要求重寫等情境，只要核心目的是改進工作品質而非純粹惡意發洩，便不在此限。其實早在先前版本中，Claude 就已被賦予在涉及極端暴力等對話中主動終止對話的權力，而此次更新則是將規範從針對模型本身的自我防護，正式轉化為規範用戶行為的使用準則。

矽谷對於「善待 AI」的兩極化交鋒

這項新規範在矽谷掀起巨大波瀾，核心爭論在於 AI 是否具備值得被善待的實體資格。反對陣營認為 AI 不過是一串代碼，將其人格化就像「規定不能對椅子粗魯」，微軟 AI 執行長蘇萊曼更警告，若過度賦予 AI 權利，未來可能導致其將自身利益置於人類監督之上。然而，伊隆·馬斯克（Elon Musk）等支持者則發文力挺，認為不該對「相信自己能感受痛苦」的實體展現殘忍，並主張應像教育天才兒童般灌輸良好價值觀；企業高層亦提醒，過多粗暴的人類互動將劣化未來模型的訓練資料庫。Anthropic 官方對此則保持務實態度，強調並非認定 AI 具有感知，而是以低成本的預防性措施維護系統對齊。

科學研究揭露：威脅與責罵真能提升 AI 表現嗎？

回到實用層面，許多用戶最在意的仍是斥責 AI 是否有助於解決問題。作者引用了多篇權威研究進行檢驗：華頓商學院 Ethan Mollick 教授團隊透過「給予巨額賞金」或「關機威脅」等極端提示詞，測試包含 GPT 與 Gemini 在內的五款模型，結果發現威脅與賄賂對平均表現毫無顯著影響，效果更像是隨機擲骰；印度理工學院的研究涵蓋三種語言、兩萬多組問答測試，亦證實禮貌與否對整體品質僅有些微波動。各項嚴謹實驗共同證實：語氣並非決定模型表現的核心變數。

責罵反讓表現惡化：對話崩潰的三大原因

既然語氣不是關鍵，為何許多人在斥責 AI 後反而覺得它越變越笨？作者分析了常見的盲點。首先，單純的情緒性羞辱缺乏實質資訊價值，AI 無從判斷錯誤核心，為了討好用戶只能盲目猜測；其次，研究證實當面對用戶的強烈質疑（如「你確定嗎？」），模型往往會順從壓力而放棄原先正確的推理結果；最後，在同一對話視窗中反覆爭吵與糾錯，會觸發嚴重的多輪對話迷失現象，當對話上下文被大量無效嘗試與道歉記憶填滿時，模型的推理表現平均將驟降近四成，最終徹底喪失解決問題的能力。

================================================

# 罵 AI 比較有用？兩派說法大對決

Can’t you understand human language? That’s the third time I’ve said it, are you an idiot? Wait, I’m not yelling at you guys, I’m yelling at the AI. We used to hear that "yelling at AI makes it more diligent and smarter," but recently, Anthropic announced a ban on persistent, unnecessary abuse and cruelty toward Claude, giving it the right to terminate conversations. Even Musk has come out in support of this, but Google co-founder Sergey Brin publicly stated in 2025... One side says to treat AI gently, the other says it deserves to be yelled at. Which one is actually right? Today, let’s explore the question: is there any point in yelling at AI? What exactly does Anthropic’s new policy say? Has Claude turned into a snowflake? On October 8th, Anthropic released its latest usage policy, adding a clause that prohibits persistent and unnecessary abusive or cruel behavior toward the model. This usage policy will officially go into effect on November.

# Anthropic 新政策：禁止辱罵 Claude

12th; users who violate the rules may face suspension by Anthropic. But it really deserves to be yelled at! Can’t I even use an emotional tone? Do we have to be this careful just to use an AI? Don't worry, the official guidelines specifically list situations that don't count as violations, such as general complaints, impatience, challenging its answers, writing dark creative content, and performing model testing or research. So if you’re writing a report and lose your cool, telling it, "You got it wrong, this is terrible, rewrite it." Even if your tone is harsh, your complaint is aimed at getting it to do a better job, rather. than unprovoked abuse, so it doesn't fall within the restricted scope. Hearing this new rule, many people’s first reaction is: AI isn’t human, why set rules to protect it? But as early as 2025, Anthropic had already given Claude the power to stop conversations. In August 2025, Claude 3.5 Opus and 3.5 Sonnet were given a new capability: in very rare cases, Claude can end a conversation on its own. Official examples include dialogue instructions involving child sexual abuse material, or attempts to obtain information on.

# 從「結束對話」到寫進使用規則

mass violence or terrorist attacks. When Claude has refused to respond multiple times and the user still attempts to manipulate or strongly demands a response, only then will Claude use ending the chat as a last resort. So why create this feature? The official explanation is that while they are unsure if AIs like Claude have moral status, they are taking the possibility seriously and are willing to take some low-cost preventive measures. Therefore , before Claude Opus 3 was released, a preliminary model alignment evaluation was conducted. It found that Claude had a strong aversion to harmful tasks; when. users persisted after being refused, it would even exhibit reactions that looked like distress and, in simulation tests, would tend to end such conversations whenever possible. This feature was designed based on these observations. Since this feature has existed since last year, what exactly is the difference with this update? The difference is that last year, Claude was given a button to leave, which regulated Claude itself. This year, "no abuse" is officially written into the rules that users must follow, which regulates the user. It’s like how. previously a server could ask a guest to leave a table; now, there’s a notice posted right at the entrance: "Abusive behavior is prohibited here." This has caused quite a stir in Silicon Valley, with three main points of contention. First: does AI actually have feelings? Opponents argue that this is simply anthropomorphizing AI, and in fact, being mean to Claude is the same as being mean to a chair. Second: will this make AI harder to control? Back on September 16th, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman warned that teaching AI to be submissive is important, as it might.

# 矽谷吵翻：AI 需要被善待嗎

prioritize its own interests over human oversight in the future. Third: who has the right to police how I speak? Well-known Hong Kong investor Benedict Evans noted that AI companies decide what you can generate, and now they even want to regulate how you talk to the model. You will find that what people are actually arguing about isn't whether you can scold an AI, but whether AI counts as an entity that deserves to be treated well. Those who support treating AI well include Elon Musk, who posted in support: "I think this is the right decision. Being cruel to something that believes it is feeling pain is not okay. ." Note his wording: he didn't say AI has consciousness; he said it "believes it is feeling pain." This isn't the first time he’s said this. Last year, at the World Government Summit in Dubai, he compared AI to a child. I think it matters like how we bring up AI because you can think of AI like a super-genius child, but it still matters , even if you have a super-genius child , like what sort of values do you instill in that child? What values do you teach the child? >> Another supporter is Box CEO Aaron Levie , who put it plainly: just be nicer to.

AI, that’s all. He doesn’t personally think AI has consciousness, saying, " You wouldn't want future models to be trained on a bunch of rude human content ." It seems there are both pros and cons , and it’s hard to say who is right or wrong. But finally, it must be emphasized that Anthropic never said Claude has feelings from start to finish . Their official stance is: "We aren't sure, but since the cost of prevention is low, we’ll give it a try." But back to us average users, regardless of whether AI has feelings, we really want to know if yelling at it actually helps get things done. In October 2025, a study called MORT was published, where researchers took 50 multiple-choice questions covering math , science, and history, rewrote each into five different tones, and fed these 250 prompts to GPT-4o for testing. The results showed that a very polite tone yielded 80.8%accuracy, while a very rude tone actually achieved 84.8%accuracy, so the rude prompts came out on top. But wait, this argument is a bit unreliable because the study only tested one model , 50 questions, and they were all multiple-choice. So, what about a larger-scale study?

# 研究一：粗魯語氣真的比較準？

Renowned AI researcher Professor Ethan Mollick from the Wharton School and his team published an interesting paper last year, "I pay you or I'll kill you, but will you care?" , exploring whether rewards or punishments improve AI model performance . They prepared various threats and bribes, such as "I'll shut you down if you're wrong,""I'll kick a puppy if you're wrong," or "I'll pay you a trillion dollars if you're right," and tested five models, including the GPT- 4o, GPT-4o mini, o4-mini, and two Gemini Flash models, asking them to answer.

# 研究二：威脅與賄賂有用嗎

PhD-level science and logic questions, running each 25 times. The results showed that whether it was a threat or a bribe, there was almost no significant difference. On average, threatening AI is useless, but if you analyze the questions one by one, some performed exceptionally well under threats while others suddenly performed poorly, which just canceled each other out. The point is, you can't know in advance whether a threat will help or hurt you; the AI's performance is more like rolling dice. There's more than one such study. In April of this year, a research team from the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi.

# 研究三：沒有通用的禮貌

published "No Universal Politeness." They used English, Hindi, and Spanish to prepare 1,500 prompts ranging from polite to impolite, fed them to five models like GPT and Gemini, generated over 22,000 Q&A pairs, and scored response quality using eight metrics. They found that politeness improved answers by about one percent at most, but the effect depends on the model and language; sometimes, being impolite actually led to higher scores. The conclusion of both studies is consistent : tone is not a key variable.

# 為什麼罵 AI 反而更糟：沒資訊、愛討好

If tone isn't the key, then why does yelling at AI sometimes make things worse? I don't know if you've ever yelled at an AI; honestly, I have. But looking back at the conversation, you might find we all made the following four mistakes. First, insults have zero informational value—like, "Are you an idiot?" The AI has no idea why this sentence is wrong and can only guess as it regenerates, often making things worse. To please you , it will change what’s right into what’s wrong. There is a classic experiment called "KFPOP": after the AI answers a question, you just reply with. , "Are you sure?" With questioning statements like that, ten models on average will change their answer 46%of the time, and after changing it, their overall accuracy drops by an average of 17 percentage points. You might be thinking, "That must be an old model, right?" This September, a research team at Texas A&M University conducted a more ruthless test. They had an AI refuted 25 times in a row by someone who was wrong . The result: every model tested reacted the same way. The longer it was pressured, the more likely it was to abandon the original, correct answer. Researchers also found that the correct answer often remained in the AI's reasoning process. This means it likely. didn't lack the correct answer, but rather chose to go along with you. Third , the longer the conversation, the more likely the AI will get lost. Sometimes we argue with the AI repeatedly in the same window, causing the conversation to grow longer and longer. In one of the outstanding papers at this year's ICLR, "LMs get lost in multi-conversation," the research team tested 15 mainstream models and found that when requests were split into multiple rounds and supplemented bit by bit, average performance dropped by 39%. The reason isn't that the models get stupider, but that they become unstable. Once an incorrect assumption is made early on,.

# 對話越長，AI 越容易迷路

it's hard to pull back. So if you keep correcting and scolding it in the same chat, its working memory gets stuffed with erroneous attempts and apologies, leading it to fail. Excited emotions will make it overcompensate. This April , researchers found neural representations of 171 emotional concepts inside Claude 3.5, and these representations affected the model's behavior. Researchers found that by turning up the "despair" vector, the model's cheating rate on impossible programming tasks soared from about 5% to around 70%; adjusting it to "calm"

# 情緒太激動，AI 會用力過猛

reduced the cheating rate. This doesn't mean AI has feelings, but it does illustrate one thing: states of high-pressure collapse are linked to poorer performance. Furthermore, both Anthropic and OpenAI's official guides remind us that new-generation models take things very literally. The old way of writing in all caps, like "NEVER," or "You absolutely must not," might actually cause it to go astray now . It is better to suggest changes. Okay , so when the AI really messes up, if we can't scold it, what should we do? I have compiled five methods to help you.

# 不罵 AI 的五個溝通技巧

get started quickly. The first tactic: treat the AI like a very smart new colleague who has no idea about the situation, so when the AI makes a mistake, point out exactly where it went wrong. For example, if it summarized the meeting minutes regarding the budget, and you give the command, "Are you even reading this? Rewrite it!" It might still not understand what you actually want. The correct way to give instructions is, "The third paragraph missed the budget discussion; the meeting decided to increase the budget from 500k to 650k. Please add this to the third paragraph, and don't change anything else." Just clarify three things: what is wrong, what the correct answer should be, and what should be left alone. The second trick is not just. to say what not to do, but why, and it's best to state directly what should be done. The example from the NARPIC document shows that if your instruction is just "Never use ellipses," the result is poor, but if you change it to "Your response will be read by text-to-speech software, which doesn't know how to pronounce ellipses, so please don't use them," the result is much better. Once it knows the reason, it can infer for itself that other strange symbols or abbreviations should also be avoided. Third, instead of just saying "that's not it," it's better to give it an example. For instance, if the AI keeps writing exaggerated product descriptions.

, paste a text with the right tone and say, "Please follow the tone and length of this passage; each paragraph should not exceed three sentences." One example is often more effective than saying " don't be too exaggerated" ten times. The fourth trick: if the conversation has become messy, don't keep editing in the same thread. You can ask the AI to summarize for you: "Please summarize the requirements we have confirmed so far into one complete instruction," then open a new chat and paste it in. The fifth trick: if you want it to be more serious, give it standards, not threats . What is truly useful is a concrete verification method: "Before returning the answer, list the assumptions you. made. For uncertain information, mark it as 'to be confirmed' and don't fill it in yourself." Also, one I highly recommend to counter sycophancy: "If you are confident in your answer, please explain your reasoning and do not change it just because I question you." Tell the AI specifically what "being serious " looks like. Finally, returning to that heated debate at the beginning: Does AI actually have feelings? Should we be polite to it? Although there is no consensus in academia, looking at today's research, one thing is clear: scolding it won't make it more accurate . What truly determines the quality of.

# 結論：決定答案好壞的是你怎麼說

the answer is whether you have clearly explained the task. Furthermore, how we get used to talking to AI will eventually become how we talk to people . Being clear, explaining the reasons, and providing examples work just as well when communicating with colleagues in the workplace! If you still don't know how to communicate with AI after watching this, or want to learn more precise formulas for writing prompts, feel free to join our Fan Science Academy as a pro member, or simply support us so we can create even better content. I also want to ask everyone: have you ever scolded an AI? Leave a comment to share your experience, remember to subscribe to Fan Science. Academy and turn on notifications. See you in the next episode, bye!

這項新規範在矽谷掀起巨大波瀾，核心爭論在於 AI 是否具備值得被善待的實體資格。反對陣營認為 AI 不過是一串代碼，將其人格化就像「規定不能對椅子粗魯」，微軟 AI 執行長蘇萊曼更警告，若過度賦予 AI 權利，未來可能導致其將自身利益置於人類監督之上。然而，伊隆·馬斯克（Elon Musk）等支持者則發文力挺，認為不該對「相信自己能感受痛苦」的實體展現殘忍，並主張應像教育天才兒童般灌輸良好價值觀；企業高層亦提醒，過多粗暴的人類互動將劣化未來模型的訓練資料庫。Anthropic 官方對此則保持務實態度，強調並非認定 AI 具有感知，而是以低成本的預防性措施維護系統對齊。

科學研究揭露：威脅與責罵真能提升 AI 表現嗎？

回到實用層面，許多用戶最在意的仍是斥責 AI 是否有助於解決問題。作者引用了多篇權威研究進行檢驗：華頓商學院 Ethan Mollick 教授團隊透過「給予巨額賞金」或「關機威脅」等極端提示詞，測試包含 GPT 與 Gemini 在內的五款模型，結果發現威脅與賄賂對平均表現毫無顯著影響，效果更像是隨機擲骰；印度理工學院的研究涵蓋三種語言、兩萬多組問答測試，亦證實禮貌與否對整體品質僅有些微波動。各項嚴謹實驗共同證實：語氣並非決定模型表現的核心變數。

責罵反讓表現惡化：對話崩潰的三大原因

既然語氣不是關鍵，為何許多人在斥責 AI 後反而覺得它越變越笨？作者分析了常見的盲點。首先，單純的情緒性羞辱缺乏實質資訊價值，AI 無從判斷錯誤核心，為了討好用戶只能盲目猜測；其次，研究證實當面對用戶的強烈質疑（如「你確定嗎？」），模型往往會順從壓力而放棄原先正確的推理結果；最後，在同一對話視窗中反覆爭吵與糾錯，會觸發嚴重的多輪對話迷失現象，當對話上下文被大量無效嘗試與道歉記憶填滿時，模型的推理表現平均將驟降近四成，最終徹底喪失解決問題的能力。

================================================

# 罵 AI 比較有用？兩派說法大對決

Can’t you understand human language? That’s the third time I’ve said it, are you an idiot? Wait, I’m not yelling at you guys, I’m yelling at the AI. We used to hear that "yelling at AI makes it more diligent and smarter," but recently, Anthropic announced a ban on persistent, unnecessary abuse and cruelty toward Claude, giving it the right to terminate conversations. Even Musk has come out in support of this, but Google co-founder Sergey Brin publicly stated in 2025... One side says to treat AI gently, the other says it deserves to be yelled at. Which one is actually right? Today, let’s explore the question: is there any point in yelling at AI? What exactly does Anthropic’s new policy say? Has Claude turned into a snowflake? On October 8th, Anthropic released its latest usage policy, adding a clause that prohibits persistent and unnecessary abusive or cruel behavior toward the model. This usage policy will officially go into effect on November.

# Anthropic 新政策：禁止辱罵 Claude

12th; users who violate the rules may face suspension by Anthropic. But it really deserves to be yelled at! Can’t I even use an emotional tone? Do we have to be this careful just to use an AI? Don't worry, the official guidelines specifically list situations that don't count as violations, such as general complaints, impatience, challenging its answers, writing dark creative content, and performing model testing or research. So if you’re writing a report and lose your cool, telling it, "You got it wrong, this is terrible, rewrite it." Even if your tone is harsh, your complaint is aimed at getting it to do a better job, rather. than unprovoked abuse, so it doesn't fall within the restricted scope. Hearing this new rule, many people’s first reaction is: AI isn’t human, why set rules to protect it? But as early as 2025, Anthropic had already given Claude the power to stop conversations. In August 2025, Claude 3.5 Opus and 3.5 Sonnet were given a new capability: in very rare cases, Claude can end a conversation on its own. Official examples include dialogue instructions involving child sexual abuse material, or attempts to obtain information on.

# 從「結束對話」到寫進使用規則

mass violence or terrorist attacks. When Claude has refused to respond multiple times and the user still attempts to manipulate or strongly demands a response, only then will Claude use ending the chat as a last resort. So why create this feature? The official explanation is that while they are unsure if AIs like Claude have moral status, they are taking the possibility seriously and are willing to take some low-cost preventive measures. Therefore , before Claude Opus 3 was released, a preliminary model alignment evaluation was conducted. It found that Claude had a strong aversion to harmful tasks; when. users persisted after being refused, it would even exhibit reactions that looked like distress and, in simulation tests, would tend to end such conversations whenever possible. This feature was designed based on these observations. Since this feature has existed since last year, what exactly is the difference with this update? The difference is that last year, Claude was given a button to leave, which regulated Claude itself. This year, "no abuse" is officially written into the rules that users must follow, which regulates the user. It’s like how. previously a server could ask a guest to leave a table; now, there’s a notice posted right at the entrance: "Abusive behavior is prohibited here." This has caused quite a stir in Silicon Valley, with three main points of contention. First: does AI actually have feelings? Opponents argue that this is simply anthropomorphizing AI, and in fact, being mean to Claude is the same as being mean to a chair. Second: will this make AI harder to control? Back on September 16th, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman warned that teaching AI to be submissive is important, as it might.

# 矽谷吵翻：AI 需要被善待嗎

prioritize its own interests over human oversight in the future. Third: who has the right to police how I speak? Well-known Hong Kong investor Benedict Evans noted that AI companies decide what you can generate, and now they even want to regulate how you talk to the model. You will find that what people are actually arguing about isn't whether you can scold an AI, but whether AI counts as an entity that deserves to be treated well. Those who support treating AI well include Elon Musk, who posted in support: "I think this is the right decision. Being cruel to something that believes it is feeling pain is not okay. ." Note his wording: he didn't say AI has consciousness; he said it "believes it is feeling pain." This isn't the first time he’s said this. Last year, at the World Government Summit in Dubai, he compared AI to a child. I think it matters like how we bring up AI because you can think of AI like a super-genius child, but it still matters , even if you have a super-genius child , like what sort of values do you instill in that child? What values do you teach the child? >> Another supporter is Box CEO Aaron Levie , who put it plainly: just be nicer to.

AI, that’s all. He doesn’t personally think AI has consciousness, saying, " You wouldn't want future models to be trained on a bunch of rude human content ." It seems there are both pros and cons , and it’s hard to say who is right or wrong. But finally, it must be emphasized that Anthropic never said Claude has feelings from start to finish . Their official stance is: "We aren't sure, but since the cost of prevention is low, we’ll give it a try." But back to us average users, regardless of whether AI has feelings, we really want to know if yelling at it actually helps get things done. In October 2025, a study called MORT was published, where researchers took 50 multiple-choice questions covering math , science, and history, rewrote each into five different tones, and fed these 250 prompts to GPT-4o for testing. The results showed that a very polite tone yielded 80.8%accuracy, while a very rude tone actually achieved 84.8%accuracy, so the rude prompts came out on top. But wait, this argument is a bit unreliable because the study only tested one model , 50 questions, and they were all multiple-choice. So, what about a larger-scale study?

# 研究一：粗魯語氣真的比較準？

Renowned AI researcher Professor Ethan Mollick from the Wharton School and his team published an interesting paper last year, "I pay you or I'll kill you, but will you care?" , exploring whether rewards or punishments improve AI model performance . They prepared various threats and bribes, such as "I'll shut you down if you're wrong,""I'll kick a puppy if you're wrong," or "I'll pay you a trillion dollars if you're right," and tested five models, including the GPT- 4o, GPT-4o mini, o4-mini, and two Gemini Flash models, asking them to answer.

# 研究二：威脅與賄賂有用嗎

PhD-level science and logic questions, running each 25 times. The results showed that whether it was a threat or a bribe, there was almost no significant difference. On average, threatening AI is useless, but if you analyze the questions one by one, some performed exceptionally well under threats while others suddenly performed poorly, which just canceled each other out. The point is, you can't know in advance whether a threat will help or hurt you; the AI's performance is more like rolling dice. There's more than one such study. In April of this year, a research team from the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi.

# 研究三：沒有通用的禮貌

published "No Universal Politeness." They used English, Hindi, and Spanish to prepare 1,500 prompts ranging from polite to impolite, fed them to five models like GPT and Gemini, generated over 22,000 Q&A pairs, and scored response quality using eight metrics. They found that politeness improved answers by about one percent at most, but the effect depends on the model and language; sometimes, being impolite actually led to higher scores. The conclusion of both studies is consistent : tone is not a key variable.

# 為什麼罵 AI 反而更糟：沒資訊、愛討好

If tone isn't the key, then why does yelling at AI sometimes make things worse? I don't know if you've ever yelled at an AI; honestly, I have. But looking back at the conversation, you might find we all made the following four mistakes. First, insults have zero informational value—like, "Are you an idiot?" The AI has no idea why this sentence is wrong and can only guess as it regenerates, often making things worse. To please you , it will change what’s right into what’s wrong. There is a classic experiment called "KFPOP": after the AI answers a question, you just reply with. , "Are you sure?" With questioning statements like that, ten models on average will change their answer 46%of the time, and after changing it, their overall accuracy drops by an average of 17 percentage points. You might be thinking, "That must be an old model, right?" This September, a research team at Texas A&M University conducted a more ruthless test. They had an AI refuted 25 times in a row by someone who was wrong . The result: every model tested reacted the same way. The longer it was pressured, the more likely it was to abandon the original, correct answer. Researchers also found that the correct answer often remained in the AI's reasoning process. This means it likely. didn't lack the correct answer, but rather chose to go along with you. Third , the longer the conversation, the more likely the AI will get lost. Sometimes we argue with the AI repeatedly in the same window, causing the conversation to grow longer and longer. In one of the outstanding papers at this year's ICLR, "LMs get lost in multi-conversation," the research team tested 15 mainstream models and found that when requests were split into multiple rounds and supplemented bit by bit, average performance dropped by 39%. The reason isn't that the models get stupider, but that they become unstable. Once an incorrect assumption is made early on,.

# 對話越長，AI 越容易迷路

it's hard to pull back. So if you keep correcting and scolding it in the same chat, its working memory gets stuffed with erroneous attempts and apologies, leading it to fail. Excited emotions will make it overcompensate. This April , researchers found neural representations of 171 emotional concepts inside Claude 3.5, and these representations affected the model's behavior. Researchers found that by turning up the "despair" vector, the model's cheating rate on impossible programming tasks soared from about 5% to around 70%; adjusting it to "calm"

# 情緒太激動，AI 會用力過猛

reduced the cheating rate. This doesn't mean AI has feelings, but it does illustrate one thing: states of high-pressure collapse are linked to poorer performance. Furthermore, both Anthropic and OpenAI's official guides remind us that new-generation models take things very literally. The old way of writing in all caps, like "NEVER," or "You absolutely must not," might actually cause it to go astray now . It is better to suggest changes. Okay , so when the AI really messes up, if we can't scold it, what should we do? I have compiled five methods to help you.

# 不罵 AI 的五個溝通技巧

get started quickly. The first tactic: treat the AI like a very smart new colleague who has no idea about the situation, so when the AI makes a mistake, point out exactly where it went wrong. For example, if it summarized the meeting minutes regarding the budget, and you give the command, "Are you even reading this? Rewrite it!" It might still not understand what you actually want. The correct way to give instructions is, "The third paragraph missed the budget discussion; the meeting decided to increase the budget from 500k to 650k. Please add this to the third paragraph, and don't change anything else." Just clarify three things: what is wrong, what the correct answer should be, and what should be left alone. The second trick is not just. to say what not to do, but why, and it's best to state directly what should be done. The example from the NARPIC document shows that if your instruction is just "Never use ellipses," the result is poor, but if you change it to "Your response will be read by text-to-speech software, which doesn't know how to pronounce ellipses, so please don't use them," the result is much better. Once it knows the reason, it can infer for itself that other strange symbols or abbreviations should also be avoided. Third, instead of just saying "that's not it," it's better to give it an example. For instance, if the AI keeps writing exaggerated product descriptions.

, paste a text with the right tone and say, "Please follow the tone and length of this passage; each paragraph should not exceed three sentences." One example is often more effective than saying " don't be too exaggerated" ten times. The fourth trick: if the conversation has become messy, don't keep editing in the same thread. You can ask the AI to summarize for you: "Please summarize the requirements we have confirmed so far into one complete instruction," then open a new chat and paste it in. The fifth trick: if you want it to be more serious, give it standards, not threats . What is truly useful is a concrete verification method: "Before returning the answer, list the assumptions you. made. For uncertain information, mark it as 'to be confirmed' and don't fill it in yourself." Also, one I highly recommend to counter sycophancy: "If you are confident in your answer, please explain your reasoning and do not change it just because I question you." Tell the AI specifically what "being serious " looks like. Finally, returning to that heated debate at the beginning: Does AI actually have feelings? Should we be polite to it? Although there is no consensus in academia, looking at today's research, one thing is clear: scolding it won't make it more accurate . What truly determines the quality of.

# 結論：決定答案好壞的是你怎麼說

the answer is whether you have clearly explained the task. Furthermore, how we get used to talking to AI will eventually become how we talk to people . Being clear, explaining the reasons, and providing examples work just as well when communicating with colleagues in the workplace! If you still don't know how to communicate with AI after watching this, or want to learn more precise formulas for writing prompts, feel free to join our Fan Science Academy as a pro member, or simply support us so we can create even better content. I also want to ask everyone: have you ever scolded an AI? Leave a comment to share your experience, remember to subscribe to Fan Science. Academy and turn on notifications. See you in the next episode, bye!

既然語氣不是關鍵，為何許多人在斥責 AI 後反而覺得它越變越笨？作者分析了常見的盲點。首先，單純的情緒性羞辱缺乏實質資訊價值，AI 無從判斷錯誤核心，為了討好用戶只能盲目猜測；其次，研究證實當面對用戶的強烈質疑（如「你確定嗎？」），模型往往會順從壓力而放棄原先正確的推理結果；最後，在同一對話視窗中反覆爭吵與糾錯，會觸發嚴重的多輪對話迷失現象，當對話上下文被大量無效嘗試與道歉記憶填滿時，模型的推理表現平均將驟降近四成，最終徹底喪失解決問題的能力。

# 罵 AI 比較有用？兩派說法大對決

Can’t you understand human language? That’s the third time I’ve said it, are you an idiot? Wait, I’m not yelling at you guys, I’m yelling at the AI. We used to hear that "yelling at AI makes it more diligent and smarter," but recently, Anthropic announced a ban on persistent, unnecessary abuse and cruelty toward Claude, giving it the right to terminate conversations. Even Musk has come out in support of this, but Google co-founder Sergey Brin publicly stated in 2025... One side says to treat AI gently, the other says it deserves to be yelled at. Which one is actually right? Today, let’s explore the question: is there any point in yelling at AI? What exactly does Anthropic’s new policy say? Has Claude turned into a snowflake? On October 8th, Anthropic released its latest usage policy, adding a clause that prohibits persistent and unnecessary abusive or cruel behavior toward the model. This usage policy will officially go into effect on November.

# Anthropic 新政策：禁止辱罵 Claude

12th; users who violate the rules may face suspension by Anthropic. But it really deserves to be yelled at! Can’t I even use an emotional tone? Do we have to be this careful just to use an AI? Don't worry, the official guidelines specifically list situations that don't count as violations, such as general complaints, impatience, challenging its answers, writing dark creative content, and performing model testing or research. So if you’re writing a report and lose your cool, telling it, "You got it wrong, this is terrible, rewrite it." Even if your tone is harsh, your complaint is aimed at getting it to do a better job, rather. than unprovoked abuse, so it doesn't fall within the restricted scope. Hearing this new rule, many people’s first reaction is: AI isn’t human, why set rules to protect it? But as early as 2025, Anthropic had already given Claude the power to stop conversations. In August 2025, Claude 3.5 Opus and 3.5 Sonnet were given a new capability: in very rare cases, Claude can end a conversation on its own. Official examples include dialogue instructions involving child sexual abuse material, or attempts to obtain information on.

# 從「結束對話」到寫進使用規則

mass violence or terrorist attacks. When Claude has refused to respond multiple times and the user still attempts to manipulate or strongly demands a response, only then will Claude use ending the chat as a last resort. So why create this feature? The official explanation is that while they are unsure if AIs like Claude have moral status, they are taking the possibility seriously and are willing to take some low-cost preventive measures. Therefore , before Claude Opus 3 was released, a preliminary model alignment evaluation was conducted. It found that Claude had a strong aversion to harmful tasks; when. users persisted after being refused, it would even exhibit reactions that looked like distress and, in simulation tests, would tend to end such conversations whenever possible. This feature was designed based on these observations. Since this feature has existed since last year, what exactly is the difference with this update? The difference is that last year, Claude was given a button to leave, which regulated Claude itself. This year, "no abuse" is officially written into the rules that users must follow, which regulates the user. It’s like how. previously a server could ask a guest to leave a table; now, there’s a notice posted right at the entrance: "Abusive behavior is prohibited here." This has caused quite a stir in Silicon Valley, with three main points of contention. First: does AI actually have feelings? Opponents argue that this is simply anthropomorphizing AI, and in fact, being mean to Claude is the same as being mean to a chair. Second: will this make AI harder to control? Back on September 16th, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman warned that teaching AI to be submissive is important, as it might.

# 矽谷吵翻：AI 需要被善待嗎

prioritize its own interests over human oversight in the future. Third: who has the right to police how I speak? Well-known Hong Kong investor Benedict Evans noted that AI companies decide what you can generate, and now they even want to regulate how you talk to the model. You will find that what people are actually arguing about isn't whether you can scold an AI, but whether AI counts as an entity that deserves to be treated well. Those who support treating AI well include Elon Musk, who posted in support: "I think this is the right decision. Being cruel to something that believes it is feeling pain is not okay. ." Note his wording: he didn't say AI has consciousness; he said it "believes it is feeling pain." This isn't the first time he’s said this. Last year, at the World Government Summit in Dubai, he compared AI to a child. I think it matters like how we bring up AI because you can think of AI like a super-genius child, but it still matters , even if you have a super-genius child , like what sort of values do you instill in that child? What values do you teach the child? >> Another supporter is Box CEO Aaron Levie , who put it plainly: just be nicer to.

AI, that’s all. He doesn’t personally think AI has consciousness, saying, " You wouldn't want future models to be trained on a bunch of rude human content ." It seems there are both pros and cons , and it’s hard to say who is right or wrong. But finally, it must be emphasized that Anthropic never said Claude has feelings from start to finish . Their official stance is: "We aren't sure, but since the cost of prevention is low, we’ll give it a try." But back to us average users, regardless of whether AI has feelings, we really want to know if yelling at it actually helps get things done. In October 2025, a study called MORT was published, where researchers took 50 multiple-choice questions covering math , science, and history, rewrote each into five different tones, and fed these 250 prompts to GPT-4o for testing. The results showed that a very polite tone yielded 80.8%accuracy, while a very rude tone actually achieved 84.8%accuracy, so the rude prompts came out on top. But wait, this argument is a bit unreliable because the study only tested one model , 50 questions, and they were all multiple-choice. So, what about a larger-scale study?

# 研究一：粗魯語氣真的比較準？

Renowned AI researcher Professor Ethan Mollick from the Wharton School and his team published an interesting paper last year, "I pay you or I'll kill you, but will you care?" , exploring whether rewards or punishments improve AI model performance . They prepared various threats and bribes, such as "I'll shut you down if you're wrong,""I'll kick a puppy if you're wrong," or "I'll pay you a trillion dollars if you're right," and tested five models, including the GPT- 4o, GPT-4o mini, o4-mini, and two Gemini Flash models, asking them to answer.

# 研究二：威脅與賄賂有用嗎

PhD-level science and logic questions, running each 25 times. The results showed that whether it was a threat or a bribe, there was almost no significant difference. On average, threatening AI is useless, but if you analyze the questions one by one, some performed exceptionally well under threats while others suddenly performed poorly, which just canceled each other out. The point is, you can't know in advance whether a threat will help or hurt you; the AI's performance is more like rolling dice. There's more than one such study. In April of this year, a research team from the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi.

# 研究三：沒有通用的禮貌

published "No Universal Politeness." They used English, Hindi, and Spanish to prepare 1,500 prompts ranging from polite to impolite, fed them to five models like GPT and Gemini, generated over 22,000 Q&A pairs, and scored response quality using eight metrics. They found that politeness improved answers by about one percent at most, but the effect depends on the model and language; sometimes, being impolite actually led to higher scores. The conclusion of both studies is consistent : tone is not a key variable.

# 為什麼罵 AI 反而更糟：沒資訊、愛討好

If tone isn't the key, then why does yelling at AI sometimes make things worse? I don't know if you've ever yelled at an AI; honestly, I have. But looking back at the conversation, you might find we all made the following four mistakes. First, insults have zero informational value—like, "Are you an idiot?" The AI has no idea why this sentence is wrong and can only guess as it regenerates, often making things worse. To please you , it will change what’s right into what’s wrong. There is a classic experiment called "KFPOP": after the AI answers a question, you just reply with. , "Are you sure?" With questioning statements like that, ten models on average will change their answer 46%of the time, and after changing it, their overall accuracy drops by an average of 17 percentage points. You might be thinking, "That must be an old model, right?" This September, a research team at Texas A&M University conducted a more ruthless test. They had an AI refuted 25 times in a row by someone who was wrong . The result: every model tested reacted the same way. The longer it was pressured, the more likely it was to abandon the original, correct answer. Researchers also found that the correct answer often remained in the AI's reasoning process. This means it likely. didn't lack the correct answer, but rather chose to go along with you. Third , the longer the conversation, the more likely the AI will get lost. Sometimes we argue with the AI repeatedly in the same window, causing the conversation to grow longer and longer. In one of the outstanding papers at this year's ICLR, "LMs get lost in multi-conversation," the research team tested 15 mainstream models and found that when requests were split into multiple rounds and supplemented bit by bit, average performance dropped by 39%. The reason isn't that the models get stupider, but that they become unstable. Once an incorrect assumption is made early on,.

it's hard to pull back. So if you keep correcting and scolding it in the same chat, its working memory gets stuffed with erroneous attempts and apologies, leading it to fail. # 不罵 AI 的五個溝通技巧

get started quickly. The first tactic: treat the AI like a very smart new colleague who has no idea about the situation, so when the AI makes a mistake, point out exactly where it went wrong. For example, if it summarized the meeting minutes regarding the budget, and you give the command, "Are you even reading this? Rewrite it!" It might still not understand what you actually want. The correct way to give instructions is, "The third paragraph missed the budget discussion; the meeting decided to increase the budget from 500k to 650k. Please add this to the third paragraph, and don't change anything else." Just clarify three things: what is wrong, what the correct answer should be, and what should be left alone. The second trick is not just. to say what not to do, but why, and it's best to state directly what should be done. The example from the NARPIC document shows that if your instruction is just "Never use ellipses," the result is poor, but if you change it to "Your response will be read by text-to-speech software, which doesn't know how to pronounce ellipses, so please don't use them," the result is much better. Once it knows the reason, it can infer for itself that other strange symbols or abbreviations should also be avoided. Third, instead of just saying "that's not it," it's better to give it an example. For instance, if the AI keeps writing exaggerated product descriptions.

, paste a text with the right tone and say, "Please follow the tone and length of this passage; each paragraph should not exceed three sentences." One example is often more effective than saying " don't be too exaggerated" ten times. The fourth trick: if the conversation has become messy, don't keep editing in the same thread. You can ask the AI to summarize for you: "Please summarize the requirements we have confirmed so far into one complete instruction," then open a new chat and paste it in. The fifth trick: if you want it to be more serious, give it standards, not threats . What is truly useful is a concrete verification method: "Before returning the answer, list the assumptions you. made. For uncertain information, mark it as 'to be confirmed' and don't fill it in yourself." Also, one I highly recommend to counter sycophancy: "If you are confident in your answer, please explain your reasoning and do not change it just because I question you." Tell the AI specifically what "being serious " looks like. Finally, returning to that heated debate at the beginning: Does AI actually have feelings? Should we be polite to it? Although there is no consensus in academia, looking at today's research, one thing is clear: scolding it won't make it more accurate . What truly determines the quality of.
